extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, law students, and news-agency legal counsel litigating unfair-competition claims
extracted.subtask_description: Transcribed court hearing and legal argument about whether and when news gathered and disseminated by a news agency constitutes protectable property and when a rival may be enjoined for appropriating and selling that news as its own. The page presents legal standards, precedent summaries, factual factors, and remedies relevant to unfair competition claims by news organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as property / intangible property entitled to equity protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that news gathered and transmitted by a news agency is 'our property' and 'just as real as if it were personal property or tangible property' and that intangible property in information is entitled to the protection of a court of equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Grosscup's and other opinions emphasize that the business 'involves, also, the use of property' and that intangible property (the compiled/timely information and the service of pre-communicatedness) may be protected by equity just as tangible property is. Examples and authorities cited include ticker and Board of Trade cases, and language that intangible qualities created by a business (exchangeability, pre-communicatedness) are 'property nevertheless.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfair competition by taking news and selling it as one's own
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking dispatches or news gathered at another's expense and selling them to customers as if gathered independently constitutes unfair competition and fraud on the competitor and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument stresses that using another's news 'as their own' deceives the public and injures the gatherer; courts have enjoined rival enterprises that 'appropriat[e] vi et armis' news and redistribute it to patrons. Repeated examples (tickers, newspapers) are used to show this is actionable unfair competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posting on bulletin/black-boards does not necessarily dedicate information to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere posting of information (on a newspaper bulletin board or a ticker/black-board in a business open to the public) is not necessarily such publication as to deprive the gatherer of all exclusive rights or to permit a rival to take and use it as its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Western Union and related cases where courts issued injunctions restraining rivals from taking information displayed on tickers or black-boards; the 'posting' context is distinguished from an unrestricted public dedication. The specific facts (who posts, to whom, and under what limitation) matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting the source can permit use of reproduced news
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rival uses news but gives credit (e.g., 'The Evening Post says so and so' or 'The Associated Press says so and so'), that practice may make the use permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and Court discussion indicate that attribution removes the deception and allows competitors to report the same facts provided the source is disclosed; Mr. Jennings concedes that saying the paper/agency is the source 'would be all right.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge/notice of the source is relevant to enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction may be difficult to enforce if the defendant does not know that the news comes from the plaintiff — defendants who lack knowledge of the proprietary source present enforcement and proof problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Jennings concedes that if the defendant 'doesn't know that it is our news' enforcement is doubtful; the defendant's officers' knowledge of particular transactions is material and is addressed by grouped affidavits in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compiled news/quotations can be protected like trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff's collection and compilation of market quotations or other information may be entitled to protection analogous to a trade secret; the compiler can keep the collected material to itself and courts may restrain those who obtain it by inducing a breach of trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Holmes and cited cases treat collections of quotations as deserving protection; even if disclosed to persons in confidential relations under contract not to publish, outsiders may be restrained from obtaining and using the knowledge through inducing breaches. Board of Trade and ticker cases are primary examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean-hands equitable defense may bar relief
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of equity may refuse injunctive relief when the plaintiff comes with 'unclean hands' (e.g., when the plaintiff's business involves illegality or contravenes public policy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eighth Circuit refusal to enjoin distribution was grounded on 'clean hands' because the Board of Trade's activities were said to include gambling/futures violations. Plaintiffs seeking equitable protection must be free from such disqualifying conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable remedy can impose a temporal exclusivity (e.g., delay before rivals may use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have fashioned injunctions restraining rivals from using compiled news or ticker information for a limited period (example: preventing use until after sixty minutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Western Union/ticker decision is discussed as involving an injunction preventing rival redistribution until after a lapse (sixty minutes cited). Such temporal restraints aim to preserve the commercial value of 'pre-communicatedness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: News/ticker matter may not be copyrightable; other legal tools required
rubrics_metrics.description: The printed tape/timely news often lacks copyrightability ('the mere annal of events') so protection cannot rest on copyright law alone; equity or other doctrines must supply a remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have distinguished these facts from authorship/publishing and noted the inadequacy of copyright law to protect ephemeral, time-sensitive information, thereby justifying equitable protection for the service provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach of contract/trust as a basis for protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Where members or affiliates are contractually limited in their use (e.g., may use dispatches only for publication in their papers and not for sale to agencies), inducing or facilitating breaches of those agreements supports equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Associated Press' arrangement with members limiting use of dispatches is cited; courts may enjoin third parties who exploit or induce breaches of such limited-right arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of misappropriation applies across assorted industries
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal principle preventing appropriation of another's labor/information has been applied in diverse contexts — theatrical dialogue, construction bid information, ticker/market quotations, phonograph record duplication, and exchange tank systems — when rival use appropriates the value created by the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many cases are cited illustrating that courts enjoin copying or appropriation where a defendant uses another's product/information/system in a manner that takes unfair advantage of the plaintiff's business, even when conventional intellectual property law (copyright, patent) does not directly apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation that destroys or seriously injures the service justifies equity
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rival can appropriate the plaintiff's expensively produced, time-sensitive information and escape the costs of collection, it could lead to the cessation or destruction of the plaintiff's business, which equity may prevent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Grosscup's opinion stresses the commercial value of earlier knowledge and that appropriation could cause 'the gathering and distributing of news, as a business enterprise, would cease altogether.' Courts weigh the risk of injurious appropriation when granting relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing private persons from competing enterprises
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordinary private person who provides news to an agency is not in the same position as a competing news enterprise; taking news from a private person does not necessarily raise unfair-competition concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court notes there is 'no question of unfair competition' where a private person gives information to a news agency; the relevant concern is commercial appropriation by competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must show a protectable investment/expense in gathering the news
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider the expense and organization (trained eyes, dispatchers, instruments, wires, etc.) the plaintiff has invested in gathering and transmitting news when assessing entitlement to protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments highlight that the service's value derives from the costly apparatus and skilled personnel that produce timely information; demonstration of that investment supports equitable protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity fills gaps where existing legal categories (authorship/ publication) don't fit modern services
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the law developed around authorship/publication is inadequate to protect new classes of commercial information services (e.g., news/ticker/telegraph enterprises), courts may develop equitable precedent to secure remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Grosscup's rhetoric urges making precedent 'one from which is eliminated... the law grown up around authorship' so that modern enterprises can appeal to the courts against 'the parasite.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting early editions of newspapers is actionable conduct at issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A core complaint is the rival's practice of rewriting stories from early newspaper editions and selling them as its own; this practice forms the factual basis for claims of appropriation and unfair competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits and grouped proof focus on instances of rewriting, bulletin-board copying, and early-edition lifting; both sides acknowledge that rewriting practices occur, and the fact-pattern of such acts is central to determining liability.
